title: How to compare the best halal catering companies in Dubai
focus: Tell each provider what documentation and preparation arrangements your guests or organisation require. Review the proposed meat and poultry, then ask about stocks, sauces, desserts and other less visible ingredients. A general assurance is not a substitute for confirmation of a specific requirement. Discuss shared equipment and any alcohol-related restrictions explicitly. If allergies are also relevant, treat them as a separate assessment. Compare the clarity of the answers before deciding which proposal meets the brief.

sections.title: Use the same questions for every provider
paragraphs: A comparison becomes more useful when each proposal answers the same brief. Give providers a consistent guest count, venue, service time and menu direction. Ask them to identify preparation, delivery, equipment, staffing and clear-down separately enough for you to understand the complete scope.

Look for evidence relevant to your occasion. A portfolio may show a style you like, but ask how that format would work at your venue and for your group. If a particular credential or operational capability is essential, request the relevant information rather than assuming it from general marketing language.

There is no universal best option for every event. Compare the clarity of the proposal, the suitability of the menu and the practical plan alongside the price. A provider who understands the brief and explains responsibilities clearly gives you a stronger basis for deciding how your event will be catered.

sections.title: Review ingredient requirements across the whole menu
paragraphs: Include halal requirements in the initial brief and explain any specific expectations about sourcing or preparation. Ask about the proposed ingredients and raise questions about sauces, stocks, desserts or other components that may not be obvious from the menu title.

If your household or organisation has particular expectations about alcohol in cooking, documentation or shared equipment, discuss them explicitly. A general description of a menu cannot replace a specific assessment of those requirements. The culinary team needs to understand what is essential before the selection is confirmed.

This detail does not need to make the menu feel restrictive. Sharing dishes, plated courses and reception bites can all be considered within a clear brief. Review the final choices together so you understand what will be served and how the agreed requirements are reflected throughout the meal.

sections.title: Give every guest a considered option
paragraphs: Collect dietary requirements before the final menu is agreed. Record how many guests each requirement applies to and distinguish preferences from allergies or other essential restrictions. A clear list helps the culinary team assess suitable dishes and the preparation arrangements they would need.

A vegetarian or vegan choice should feel like a complete part of the menu. Consider its portion, accompaniments and presentation alongside the other dishes, rather than removing an ingredient and assuming the result will be satisfying. Sauces, garnishes, breads and desserts also need attention.

Allergy requests require a specific discussion of ingredients and kitchen conditions. Labels and separate serving utensils can support a plan, but they do not by themselves guarantee the absence of cross-contact. Share the details early so the team can assess the request honestly and confirm what can be accommodated before you book.

sections.title: Choose a regional direction before expanding the selection
paragraphs: A broad cuisine name can cover many different dishes and traditions. Share the region, flavours or family favourites you have in mind so the chef can build a menu with a clear identity. If there are particular ingredients or preparations you expect, describe them rather than relying only on a familiar dish name.

A focused menu often feels more coherent than a long list of unrelated favourites. Think about how starters, main dishes, sides and desserts complement one another, and how they will be served. The menu should offer enough variety for the group while remaining practical for the kitchen and service format.

Tell us about spice preferences and essential dietary requirements early. These may affect the choice of dishes as well as individual recipes. The final selection can then reflect the food you enjoy with a clear understanding of what will be prepared for your occasion.

sections.title: Compare the complete proposal
paragraphs: Read the price together with the menu and service scope. Two proposals can have different totals because one includes equipment, staffing or a longer service period that the other does not. Compare them against the same guest count and requirements before deciding which is the better fit.

Check the minimum order, included hours, delivery or transport arrangements and how applicable VAT is shown. If the menu uses a starting price, ask which choices could change it. Premium ingredients, additional stations, extended service and extra hospitality support may need separate pricing.

The written proposal should also explain the payment schedule and the terms for changes or cancellation. Use the terms attached to your booking, as a private occasion and a corporate contract may have different arrangements. A clear comparison gives you confidence in the decision and helps avoid assumptions about what a headline price includes.

sections.title: A clear brief gives the menu a better starting point
paragraphs: Start with the date, venue and number of guests, then describe how you want the occasion to feel. A working lunch, an evening reception and a family celebration need different menus and service rhythms. Tell us when people will eat, whether they will be seated or standing and which parts of the event you would like myCHEF to handle.

Include essential dietary requirements and the facilities available at the venue. A brief does not need to be long, but it should distinguish what is essential from what would simply be nice to have. If you have a spending range, share it alongside the scope so the proposal can prioritise the right elements.

We can then discuss a suitable format, food selection and staffing plan. Your written proposal brings those decisions together, giving you a clear reference for what is included before you confirm the booking.
